Part 1 · hydrogen separation

Why the H₂ packs stand outside

Leak

H₂ burns from 4 to 75 % in air; a spark ignites it.

Distance

Keep packs away from openings and hot surfaces.

Criterion here

m, assumed: typical of NFPA 2 / NFPA 55 tables for small systems.

A louvred wall is an opening: leaked H₂ can drift through it.

Part 1 · hydrogen separation

Separation checker

Now measure it: pack edge to the nearest edge of each opening or hot item.

At the assumed positions closer than 5 m; moving the packs m west clears them all.

Part 1 · summary

What part 1 settled

  • The document set has no plot plan; positions are scaled from the 3D model.
  • One origin (grid 1/A) ties plan, section and isometric together.
  • Layers keep the plot plan readable.
  • The H₂ packs sit within 5 m of the louvred wall and the heaters.

Part 2 · Elevations, platforms and escape

Are the platforms, stairs and escape routes high, steep and short enough?

Part 2 · the plan

Heights and the way out

  1. Section A–Athe skid seen from the south, every height on it
  2. Height rulesloading nozzle, headroom, stair pitch
  3. Platform checkermove a platform and watch the rules
  4. Escapetravel distance and common path from the upper platform

Part 2 · section A–A

Section A–A, looking north

Heights

Catalyst goes in through N3 near the top of R-601, so the upper platform exists for loading.

Part 2 · height rules

Three rules for the heights

Loading nozzle

N3 0.5–1.5 m above the standing floor (assumed).

Headroom

≥ 2.1 m clear under a platform's 0.2 m steel (typical).

Stair pitch

30–45°: steeper is a ladder, flatter wastes floor (ISO 14122-3).

The three rules pull against each other: a higher platform eases headroom but can bury N3 and steepen the stair.

Part 2 · platform checker

Move the platforms and R-601

Apply all three rules at once while the heights move.

The lower platform sits exactly at the 2.1 m headroom limit: lowering it 5 cm fails headroom.

Part 2 · escape

Two distances decide an escape route

Travel distance
walk from the farthest point to an exit door
m
Common path
the part walked before a second route exists
m
Rectilinear
walking along aisles: |Δx| + |Δy|, not the straight line
m
Stair flight
slope length, √(run² + rise²)
m

Limits are assumed typical values (NFPA 101 for high-hazard areas): one stair means the whole way down is a common path.

Part 2 · escape

Escape-route calculator

Second way down

The route passes the limits, but a fire at the stair foot (IBC, T-301) blocks the only way: a ladder cuts the common path.

Part 2 · summary

What part 2 settled

  • N3 sits 0.68 m above the upper platform: good for loading.
  • Both stairs are near 40°; lower-platform headroom is exactly 2.1 m.
  • Escape from the upper platform is 20.9 m, all of it common path.
  • A fixed ladder would give a second way down.

Part 3 · Isometrics, materials and access

How does an isometric turn a P&ID line into a cut list?

Part 3 · the plan

From a line number to a cut list

  1. Isometric projectionthree axes at 120°, true lengths written on
  2. Line explorerfifteen lines with their routes and fittings
  3. Bill of materialslength, bends, tees, valves and supports per line
  4. Accesscan an operator reach every gauge and valve?

Part 3 · isometric projection

A 3D route drawn on paper

$$u=(x+y)\cos 30^{\circ},\qquad v=(x-y)\sin 30^{\circ}-z$$
$x,\,y,\,z$
plant coordinates: east, north, up
m
$u,\,v$
paper coordinates: right, down
m

The picture is not to scale along every direction, so each run carries its true length in mm.

Part 3 · line explorer

Isometric of a line, with its bill of materials

Count from the route: every direction change is a bend, every branch a tee, every in-line valve two compression ends.

Part 3 · bill of materials

From route length to stock lengths

The isometric gives the length; purchasing needs whole lengths.

$$L_{buy}=1.10\,L_{route},\qquad n=\left\lceil L_{buy}/L_{stock}\right\rceil$$
$L_{route}$
sum of the run lengths on the isometric
m
1.10
cutting and bending allowance, assumed
—
$L_{stock}$
supplied length: 6.1 m tubing, 6 m pipe (assumed)
m
$n$
lengths ordered

Part 3 · bill of materials

Where the tube goes

Sort

The chilled-water pair is % of all tube: the chiller stands at the north wall, far from E-602.

Part 3 · access

Can the operator reach it?

Show

Height is measured above the floor the operator stands on: grade or a platform. Three cut-off valves sit at 1.9–2.0 m.

Part 3 · findings

Seven layout findings

Each finding is computed from the assumed layout; it becomes a query to the contractor until a plot plan confirms or clears it.

Part 3 · summary

What part 3 settled

  • An isometric writes the true length on every run.
  • Bends, tees and fittings are counted from the route.
  • Fifteen lines need about 153 m of tube; chilled water takes the most.
  • Height is judged above the operator's own floor.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Ask for a plot plan, sections and isometrics; until then, label positions assumed.

2

Measure hydrogen separation to openings and hot surfaces, not only to walls.

3

Check every platform against nozzle height, headroom, stair pitch and escape together.

4

Build the cut list from the isometric: length, bends, branches and valves.
